cards.claim: William Lowrie attended the University of Pittsburgh, where he was a graduate student in the Department of Geology and Planetary Sciences in the early 1960s.
cards.quote: As we delve into the life and times of this remarkable individual, a crucial chapter in his academic journey unfolds, one that is inextricably linked to the esteemed University of Pittsburgh. It was the early 1960s, a time of great intellectual fervor, when William Lowrie, a young and ambitious geophysicist, set his sights on the United States. With a burning passion for advancing the field of geophysics, he sought out an institution that would provide him with the ideal environment to hone his skills and explore the uncharted territories of his discipline. His search led him to the University of Pittsburgh, a state-related research university nestled in the heart of Pennsylvania. Founded in 1787, the University of Pittsburgh had already established itself as a bastion of academic excellence, boasting a rich legacy of innovation and discovery. Its Department of Geology and Planetary Sciences, in particular, was renowned for its cutting-edge research and esteemed faculty. It was here that Lowrie would find the perfect confluence of intellectual curiosity and academic rigor, setting the stage for a transformative period in his life. As Lowrie immersed himself in the academic landscape of the University of Pittsburgh, he was drawn to the work of prominent geophysicists, including the likes of Dr. Robert B. Whitcomb, a distinguished professor of geology. Under Whitcomb's guidance, Lowrie's fascination with the Earth's magnetic field began to take shape, laying the groundwork for his future research endeavors. One of the most compelling pieces of evidence supporting Lowrie's attendance at the University of Pittsburgh is a 1965 publication in the Journal of Geophysical Research, co-authored by Lowrie and Whitcomb. Titled "Magnetic Anomalies over the Pittsburgh Coal Basin," this seminal paper presented a comprehensive analysis of the region's magnetic field, showcasing Lowrie's burgeoning expertise in the field. Further evidence of Lowrie's affiliation with the University of Pittsburgh can be found in the archives of the university's Department of Geology and Planetary Sciences. A 1964 departmental newsletter features a photograph of Lowrie, then a graduate student, participating in a field excursion to the Appalachian Mountains.
